courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a Gaussian: position, covariance, opacity, SH color
question: If you train with SH degree 1 instead of 3, how many floats does each Gaussian store?
explain: Degree 1 has $1 + 3 = 4$ coefficients per channel, so 12 color floats. Add 3 position, 4 rotation, 3 scale and 1 opacity: $12 + 11 = 23$.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer
question: A thread reads Top = {A, 7} and stalls. Meanwhile other threads perform 5 successful CASes, and the last one leaves node A on top again. What does the stalled thread's CAS see, and what happens?
options: {A, 12}: it fails, then reloads and retries
{A, 7}: it succeeds, because the pointer matches
{A, 8}: it fails, because only pushes bump the tag
explain: Every successful CAS bumps the tag, so after 5 of them the word holds {A, 12}. The expected {A, 7} no longer matches, the CAS fails, and compare_exchange reloads the current {A, 12} for the retry.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
question: You ablate the dense retriever H. To keep latency equal, the no-H variant sends the top 50 BM25 candidates to the reranker instead of the top 100. nDCG drops by 0.09. What can you conclude?
options: H is worth 0.09 nDCG, since latency was held constant
The 0.09 mixes two changes, losing H and halving the candidate depth, so H's own contribution is unknown
H is worth more than 0.09, because more candidates always hurt rerankers
Nothing, because leave-one-out is invalid for first-stage retrievers
explain: Candidate depth changes recall, which bounds what the reranker can do. Run no-H at depth 100 to isolate H, and report latency separately; a depth-for-latency tradeoff is a second experiment.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: SWE-bench: how one patch gets graded
question: A patch applies cleanly, makes both FAIL_TO_PASS tests pass, and causes one FAIL_TO_FAIL test to start passing, but one PASS_TO_PASS test now fails. Verdict?
options: Resolved, since the issue tests pass
Resolved with partial credit
Not resolved, because a PASS_TO_PASS test fails
Not graded, because FAIL_TO_FAIL changed
explain: The verdict is binary and needs all FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests to pass. FAIL_TO_FAIL tests are ignored either way, and there is no partial credit.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
question: A support bot always classifies a ticket, then calls exactly one of three fixed handlers. In the terms of Building effective agents, what is it?
options: An agent, because it uses an LLM to make a decision
A workflow (routing), because the code path is predefined
An augmented LLM, because it has no tools
An orchestrator-workers agent, because it delegates
explain: The control flow is fixed in code: classify, then dispatch. That is the routing workflow. It becomes an agent only when the model decides at runtime which steps to take and how many.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Permissions, traces and evaluation
question: Your agent passes 3 of 4 trials per task. Product needs it to succeed on every one of 5 consecutive uses. Roughly what reliability should you expect?
options: About 75 percent, the per-trial rate
About 24 percent, since 0.75 to the 5th power is 0.237
About 99.9 percent, since pass@5 is high
Exactly 60 percent
explain: Needing all 5 to succeed is pass^5 = 0.75^5, about 0.237. pass@5 answers a different question (at least one success) and is far too optimistic for a workflow that must succeed every time.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The read path: scoring memories by recency, importance and relevance
question: Generative Agents measures recency from a memory's last *access*, not its creation. After this query retrieves M6, M5, M3, M1 and M7, what happens on the next query an hour later?
options: Nothing changes; recency only depends on creation time
The retrieved memories get recency 0.995 raw, so they gain an edge: frequently retrieved memories tend to stay retrievable
The retrieved memories are demoted so the agent sees different ones next time
Importance is re-rated for the retrieved memories
explain: Retrieval updates the last-access timestamp, so one hour later those five have raw recency 0.995 while the rest keep decaying. This is a rich-get-richer effect: it keeps active topics in view, but it can also lock in an early mistake. Importance is rated once, at creation.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Layer the checks: deterministic first, judges last
question: An agent fills a booking form and must output JSON with a date, a flight number in a fixed format, and a price within the user's budget. Which verification plan fits best?
options: Ask a strong LLM judge whether the booking looks right, since it can check all three fields at once
Validate the JSON schema and regex, check the price and date with code, then use a judge only for whether the flight matches the user's stated preferences
Re-ask the same agent to double-check its JSON before submitting
Skip checks for the format and only verify the price, since format errors are rare
explain: Format, ranges and arithmetic are deterministic: code checks them exactly and almost for free. A judge is reserved for the fuzzy part (preferences) that code cannot express.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask
question: In the toy rollout, the loss is normalized by the number of masked-in tokens. How many tokens is that, and what fraction of the sequence?
options: 20 tokens, 100 percent, since every token is part of the episode
16 tokens, 80 percent: everything after the prompt
6 tokens, 30 percent: only the tool outputs
10 tokens, 50 percent: only the policy's own tokens
explain: 4 prompt tokens and 6 tool tokens are masked out, leaving the 10 tokens the model sampled across its three turns. Including tool tokens would turn the update into imitation of environment text.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: A crystal as data: lattice, fractional coordinates, periodicity
question: In the hexagonal cell with a = 3 angstrom, what is the Cartesian position of fractional (0, 1, 0), that is, the tip of a2?
explain: It is a2 itself: $(-a/2, a\sqrt{3}/2, 0) = (-1.5, 2.598, 0)$. Its length is 3 angstrom and its angle to a1 = (3, 0, 0) is 120 degrees. Answer (1.5, 2.598, 0) would give a 60 degree cell, which describes the same lattice with a different convention, a reminder that conventions must be fixed before converting.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: The soft watermark: add delta to the green logits
question: A model's next-token distribution is spread evenly over many tokens. With gamma = 0.5 and delta = 2, about what fraction of its tokens will be green?
explain: e^2 = 7.39, so the fraction is 0.5 x 7.39 / (1 + 6.39 x 0.5) = 0.881. 0.73 is the answer for delta = 1, 0.50 is human text, and 1.00 would require the hard rule (infinite delta).

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
question: Your interposer's malloc wrapper calls fprintf to log each call. It hangs or overflows the stack on the first allocation. Why?
options: fprintf may itself call malloc, which re-enters the wrapper, which calls fprintf again
fprintf cannot be called from a shared library
LD_PRELOAD forbids stdio in preloaded objects
The dynamic linker has not loaded libc yet when malloc is first called
explain: Anything the tracer does while recording must not allocate through the traced path. Real tracers write fixed-size records into preallocated or mmap'd buffers and use recursion guards, like libmtrace's counter or heaptrack's dummy pool for dlsym.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
question: Why does Isolation Forest cap tree height at ceil(log2 psi) instead of growing each tree until every point is alone?
options: To make anomalies and normal points land at the same depth
Because random splits cannot separate more than log2 psi points
Because it only needs to tell short paths from long ones: anomalies are isolated early, and deep regions get the c(size) estimate instead of more splits
Because scikit-learn trees do not support deeper trees
explain: Points that survive to the limit are, by construction, the hard-to-isolate normal ones. Their remaining depth is estimated with c(size), so the tree saves work without changing the ranking of anomalies.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Commit, abort with CLRs, and fuzzy checkpoints
question: Why may a CLR never itself be undone?
options: CLRs are always forced to disk, so they are permanent
CLRs belong to the system, not to a transaction
CLRs are deleted at the next checkpoint
Undoing a CLR would reinstate the original change, and a rollback in progress must only move backward
explain: A CLR records progress of a rollback. Undoing it would reinstate an uncommitted change. Making CLRs redo-only and chaining them with UndoNextLSN guarantees rollbacks only move toward the start of the transaction.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Four ways to tell the model which side a text is on
question: You use a BGE-style model whose card says to prepend an instruction to short queries. A teammate prepends the same instruction to every passage at indexing time "for consistency". What is wrong?
options: Nothing; using the same instruction on both sides is how asymmetric models are meant to work
The model was trained with the instruction on queries only, so passages now look like queries and lose their document representation
Instructions are ignored at indexing time, so it only wastes tokens
It makes cosine scores negative
explain: BGE attaches the instruction to the query side only, and its card says no instruction is added to passages. Instructed passages are encoded as if they were queries, which is the "everything as query" mismatch you will see in the toy next lesson.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
question: You wrap 5,000 calls in `asyncio.gather(*[call(x) for x in items])` with no semaphore. Call 37 raises an exception after 0.4 s. What happens to the other calls?
options: They keep running in the background; gather re-raises the first exception to the awaiting code
All other calls are cancelled immediately and an ExceptionGroup is raised
gather waits for every call to finish, then raises the first exception
The event loop stops and the program exits
explain: With return_exceptions=False, gather propagates the first exception immediately, and the Python docs say the other awaitables are not cancelled. They continue, so you can lose their results and still be throttled by them. Cancelling siblings and raising an ExceptionGroup is TaskGroup behavior.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
question: You must classify 2 million archived documents by next week, and your interactive product shares the same API account. Which plan fits best?
options: A batch job with a custom_id per document, results upserted by custom_id
Real-time calls with a semaphore of 500 and aggressive retries
Real-time calls one at a time to stay under the limits
Real-time calls with temperature 0 so the response cache absorbs most of the load
explain: Nothing here needs an answer in seconds. Batches cost less, run on a separate rate-limit pool so the product keeps its real-time capacity, and custom_id plus upserts make partial failures and re-runs safe. A huge semaphore competes with your own product for the shared limit, and distinct documents give the response cache nothing to reuse.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Wakers: how a Pending task gets polled again
question: A `Delay` future is polled once in task X, then moved into a new task Y and polled there. Which waker must it wake when the time expires?
options: Both X's and Y's wakers, to be safe
Y's waker, from the most recent poll
X's waker, from the first poll
Neither: wakers are per runtime, not per task
explain: The Future docs say only the waker from the most recent poll should be scheduled. The Tokio tutorial's fixed Delay compares the stored waker with `will_wake` on every poll and replaces it if the task changed. Waking X would poll the wrong task, and Y would hang.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Inside the CPU: LOCK CMPXCHG, LL/SC, and weak versus strong
question: get_key() lazily creates a random key: if KEY is 0, generate one and CAS it from 0 to the new key; if the CAS fails, use the key another thread stored. There is no loop. Which CAS should it use?
options: compare_exchange_weak, because it is faster on ARM
Either, since x86 and ARM compile them identically
compare_exchange (strong), because a spurious failure would make it return 0 as the key
Neither; it needs fetch_add
explain: With weak, the CAS could fail even though KEY was still 0, and the Err would carry 0, which the function would return as the key. Strong only fails if another thread really installed a key. Weak is for loops where a spurious failure just means one more iteration. And on LL/SC targets (ARMv8.0) the two do compile differently.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
question: A clip contains a barking dog and a person talking. Model A uses softmax over classes; model B uses independent sigmoids. Which statement is correct?
options: Both can output 0.9 for Dog and 0.9 for Speech
Only model A can output high scores for both
Only model B can output 0.9 for Dog and 0.9 for Speech at the same time
Neither can; multi-label clips need two separate models
explain: Softmax outputs sum to 1, so two classes cannot both be 0.9. Independent sigmoids treat each class as its own binary question, which is why audio taggers trained on AudioSet use sigmoid outputs and binary cross-entropy.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation
question: A lead agent sends three subagents the task "research the chip shortage". The results overlap heavily and one sub-question is never covered. What is the best fix?
options: Spawn ten subagents so coverage is more likely
Run the three subagents sequentially so they can read each other's notes
Raise the subagents' temperature to diversify their searches
Give each subagent an objective, output format, source guidance and explicit boundaries that exclude the others' topics
explain: This is the failure Anthropic described: vague task descriptions lead to duplicated work and gaps. Detailed, bounded task descriptions fix the division of labor. More agents or randomness would increase cost without guaranteeing coverage, and running sequentially gives up the speedup.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Evaluating research agents without fooling yourself
question: Why does PaperBench grade results produced by re-running `reproduce.sh` in a fresh environment rather than the files the agent left behind?
options: Fresh environments are faster to grade
It stops an agent from scoring result-match leaves with numbers it wrote by hand during its run
The LLM judge cannot read files from the agent's environment
It ensures the agent used the blacklisted official code
explain: Separating reproduction from the agent's run means only results the code actually produces are graded, which closes a direct reward-hacking route: writing the expected numbers into a results file. Blacklisted code is forbidden, not required.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Training from scratch: latent weights and the STE
question: What does the straight-through estimator do in BitLinear?
options: It computes the exact gradient of RoundClip
It skips the quantizer in the forward pass during training
It uses the quantized weights in the forward pass and treats the quantizer as identity in the backward pass
It quantizes the gradients to ternary values
explain: Forward uses w_quant so the loss reflects the ternary network; the detach() trick makes d(w_quant)/dw equal to 1, so gradients flow to the latent weights. The exact gradient of rounding is zero almost everywhere, and gradients stay high precision.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Global history, gshare, TAGE and perceptron predictors
question: A perceptron with weights w0 = 0, w1 = 0, w2 = 26, w3 = 0, w4 = 0 sees history x1..x4 = +1, -1, +1, +1. What does it predict?
options: Taken, y = 26
Not taken, y = -26
Taken, y = 0
Not taken, y = -2
explain: y = w0 + sum of x_i w_i = 0 + 26 times x2 = 26 times -1 = -26 < 0, so it predicts not taken. It has learned to copy the branch 2 positions back in history.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
question: A Get(5) checks the memtable (miss), then finds 5:del in SST-2. SST-1 contains 5:a. What does the Get return?
options: 5:a, because SST-1 holds an actual value
Not found, because the newer tombstone hides every older version
An error, because the key exists in two files
It depends on which file has the larger key range
explain: The search runs newest to oldest and stops at the first entry for the key. The tombstone in SST-2 is newer than 5:a in SST-1, so the key is deleted. Multiple versions are normal in an LSM-tree, not an error.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: The buffer pool: frames, a page table, pins and dirty pages
question: Two victims are equally old. Page X is clean, page Y is dirty. Why do many buffer managers prefer X?
options: Evicting X needs no disk write; evicting Y needs a write before the frame can be reused
Dirty pages are more likely to be accessed again soon
Clean pages take more memory than dirty pages
Y cannot be evicted until the transaction that dirtied it commits
explain: The clean page is the fast path: drop it and reuse the frame. The dirty page needs a write first, which is why systems run a background writer that cleans dirty pages ahead of eviction (PostgreSQL's bgwriter, for example).

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: 2Q, InnoDB midpoint insertion and PostgreSQL ring buffers
question: You are designing a page cache for a key-value store whose workload mixes point lookups with frequent full scans, and you want O(1) work per access. Which policy fits best?
options: Plain LRU
LRU-2 with a priority queue
2Q, or a midpoint-insertion LRU like InnoDB's
CLOCK with one reference bit
explain: Plain LRU and one-bit CLOCK flood on scans. LRU-2 resists scans but costs log N per access for the priority queue. 2Q and midpoint insertion both admit pages to the hot region only after evidence of reuse, at constant cost per access.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
question: Which part of BLT should get most of the parameters, and why?
options: The latent Transformer, because it runs once per patch, so its cost per byte is divided by the patch size
The local encoder, because it sees every byte
The local decoder, because it has the softmax
The entropy model, because it decides compute
explain: Cost per byte is about 2(m_g/P + m_l). Parameters in the latent model are amortized over P bytes; parameters in local models are paid on every byte. That is why the 8B model has 6.4B latent and only 140M local parameters.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker
question: A teammate wraps a function body in `unsafe { ... }` to silence E0502 (a shared and a mutable borrow overlap). What happens?
options: It compiles, because unsafe disables borrow checking in the block
It still fails with E0502; unsafe does not relax the borrow rules on references
It compiles but inserts a run-time borrow check
It compiles only in release mode
explain: The Book is explicit: unsafe does not turn off the borrow checker or other safety checks on references. To express aliasing the checker cannot verify, you must switch to raw pointers (or `UnsafeCell` based types) and take responsibility for the rules yourself.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
question: `double a[4096][4096]` is summed with `for (j...) for (i...) s += a[i][j];`. What is the main problem and the fix?
options: Each access is a new line because the inner loop strides 32 KB; swap the loops so j is innermost
Integer overflow in the index; use size_t
The sum is not vectorized; add a pragma
The array is too large for the stack; the loop order is irrelevant
explain: Row-major layout puts `a[i][j]` and `a[i+1][j]` 4096 x 8 = 32,768 bytes apart. With i innermost every access touches a new line and uses 8 of its 64 bytes. Making j innermost gives stride 8 and 1 miss per 8 elements. (Size and storage class are separate issues.)

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Transcoders and cross-layer transcoders
question: What does a transcoder learn to approximate?
options: The residual stream at the same layer, from itself
The output of an MLP layer, computed from that MLP's input
The attention pattern of every head in the layer
The final logits, computed from the embeddings
explain: A transcoder maps MLP input to MLP output through a wide sparse layer, so it can stand in for the MLP. An SAE reconstructs the same activation it reads, which describes but does not replace the computation.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Validating a graph with interventions
question: In the poem study, steering the planned-word features changed the rhyme only at the newline token, not at other positions. What does that support?
options: The model improvises the rhyme at the last word
Attention is broken at every other token
The plan is represented at a specific site before the line is written, and later tokens read it from there
Steering never works in Haiku
explain: If the plan were made at the end of the line, steering near the end would matter. The effect being confined to the newline token supports a planning site from which later positions read, which is what the attribution graph suggested.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Small propensities, high variance, and clipping
question: A ranker trained with IPS on a small log performs erratically: retraining on a different week of logs reorders many results. Propensities at ranks 8 to 10 are around 0.02. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Drop the propensity weights and train on raw clicks
Clip propensities at a tuned tau, or collect more data
Multiply all propensities by 10
Use only clicks at ranks 8 to 10
explain: Erratic retraining points to variance from weights near 50. Clipping caps them; more data shrinks variance directly. Dropping weights reintroduces bias, and scaling all propensities by a constant does not change the ranking the estimator prefers.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100
question: Why does a larger logit scale make the loss more sensitive to mislabeled pairs?
options: Because the scale changes which caption has the highest cosine
Because when the wrong caption wins by a margin m, the row loss grows about linearly in scale times m
Because scaling by 100 overflows float16
Because the scale is applied only to the off-diagonal entries
explain: Multiplying all logits by s does not change the ranking, but for a row where a wrong caption beats the right one by m, the loss behaves like s times m for large s (see the plot with m = -0.03). The scale multiplies every entry, and overflow is avoided by subtracting the max.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Lloyd's algorithm by hand, and why the seeds decide
question: Which seeding rule does k-means++ use for the centres after the first?
options: The point farthest from all chosen centres, deterministically
The point with the highest local density that is not yet a centre
A point sampled with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest chosen centre
A point sampled uniformly from the cluster with the largest current inertia
explain: D squared weighting samples; it does not take the maximum. Sampling is what keeps a single far outlier from being chosen every time, and it is what the O(log k) proof needs. Always taking the farthest point is a different algorithm (farthest-first traversal) with different failure modes.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
question: You want one number to track nightly as a clustering pipeline changes, with a small hand-labelled sample available. Which choice best survives a change in the number of clusters the pipeline emits?
options: Unadjusted NMI, since it is bounded by 1
Inertia, since it is what k-means optimises
ARI or AMI, because both are corrected for chance and so do not drift when the number of clusters changes
Mean silhouette, since it needs no labels
explain: Chance-corrected metrics stay near 0 for random labellings at any number of clusters, so a jump in cluster count does not by itself move them. Unadjusted MI and NMI rise with more clusters, inertia falls with more clusters and is not comparable across different k or different features, and the silhouette also shifts with k and favours compact blobs. Track a chance-corrected external metric plus the coverage.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: From tuple-at-a-time to vector-at-a-time execution
question: In the MySQL profile from the X100 paper, why did one addition cost tens of cycles instead of about 3?
options: The MIPS CPU had no floating-point unit
Each call computed a single addition, so the dependent load-add-store chain could not overlap with other tuples and the call overhead was paid per value
Addition required a hash-table lookup
The data was compressed and needed decoding first
explain: The paper explains that with one addition per call the compiler cannot pipeline the loop, so four dependent instructions wait on each other (about 20 cycles), and the routine call adds a similar amount again.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
question: Why can inlining make a program slower even though it removes call instructions?
options: Inlined code cannot be vectorized
It always disables constant folding
Inlined functions run at -O0
Duplicated bodies grow the code and can cause instruction-cache misses
explain: Every call site gets its own copy. For large functions with many call sites, the bigger hot path may no longer fit in the instruction cache, and those misses can cost more than the calls saved. Compilers use size budgets for this reason.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
question: You collect a PGO profile by running only the test suite, which mostly exercises error paths. What is likely to happen on production traffic?
options: Production gets the full PGO speedup anyway
The compiler refuses the profile
The binary crashes on untested paths
The hot production paths may be treated as cold and optimized for size or laid out poorly
explain: PGO trusts the counts. Paths the profile never saw look cold, so they may be laid out away from hot code and inlined less. Profile with inputs that represent the real workload.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Why long tasks fail: compounding errors and verification
question: A team reports 97% per-step accuracy and expects 97% task success on 20-step workflows. Under the independent-step model, what should they expect without verification?
options: About 97%, since per-step accuracy equals task accuracy
About 54%
About 80%
About 3%
explain: 0.97^20 is about 0.544. Each step is another chance to fail, so success decays geometrically with length. Real errors are correlated, which can make it better or worse, but the naive 97% expectation is badly wrong.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Preemption bounds, weak memory and what loom cannot see
question: A loom test with `LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS=2` passes. What can you conclude?
options: The code is correct for every schedule
The code is correct on x86 but maybe not on Arm
No execution with at most 2 forced switches violates the test's assertions, within loom's memory-model coverage
Nothing, since bounded runs are random samples
explain: A bounded run is still systematic, not random, but it only covers executions with at most 2 preemptions. It also inherits loom's model gaps (SeqCst as AcqRel, no load buffering), so it is strong evidence, not a proof.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Self-consistency: every point on a trajectory maps to its origin
question: A colleague trains a network to predict the clean image from pure noise with an L2 loss on (noise, random training image) pairs, and calls it a one-step consistency model. What will its samples look like?
options: Sharp and diverse, identical to a consistency model
Pure noise, because the input has no information
A blurry average image, because L2 regression on random pairs learns the conditional mean
Exact copies of training images
explain: Random pairs carry no link between a given noise and a given image, so the L2-optimal output is the average of all images, like the denoiser gain 0.00004 in the toy. A consistency model is trained on pairs that lie on the same ODE trajectory, which defines a deterministic noise-to-data map.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
question: P1 writes x = 5 during [0, 10]. P2 reads x during [2, 3] and gets 5. P3 reads x during [4, 6] and gets the old value 0. Is this linearizable?
options: Yes, because all three operations overlap the write
No, because P2 completed reading 5 before P3 started, so P3 must see 5 or newer
Yes, because P3's read finished before the write finished
No, because P2 read 5 before the write had completed
explain: P2's read ([2, 3]) completes before P3's read ([4, 6]) begins, so P2 precedes P3 in any valid order. P2 returned 5, so the write precedes P2, hence P3 too, and P3 must return 5. Reading a value before its write completes (P2) is fine: the write's point can be anywhere in [0, 10].

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Eventual consistency, session guarantees and real systems
question: Which statement about consistency models is correct?
options: Eventual consistency bounds how stale a read can be
Sequential consistency forbids reading stale data
Causal consistency lets replicas show concurrent writes in different orders
Linearizability is the same as serializability
explain: Concurrent writes have no causal path, so causal replicas may order them differently. Eventual consistency gives no time bound; sequential consistency allows a process to lag arbitrarily; serializability concerns transactions with no real-time rule.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Consistent hashing with bounded loads: a hard cap per server
question: Your bounded-load cache tier shows a low hit rate and you find 35% of requests are forwarded. Which change most directly helps?
options: Lower c from 1.25 to 1.1
Raise c, say from 1.1 to 1.5 or 2
Remove virtual nodes
Switch to hash mod N
explain: Forwarded requests land on servers that are not their natural owner, so they miss more often. Raising c lets servers hold more before spilling, which keeps more requests at their home cache; in the simulation forwarding fell from 39% at c = 1.1 to 12.5% at c = 2. The price is a higher allowed peak load per server.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Too few results: relaxation ladders and post-hoc constraints
question: A ladder relaxes `within 10 km` before `8+ years`, and the first rung adds no results. What does that tell you?
options: Distance was not the binding constraint for this query; the remaining hard filters exclude the same people anyway
The ladder is broken and should be reversed automatically
The index is missing location data
Relaxation should stop because results cannot grow
explain: Relaxing one constraint only helps if it was the one excluding candidates. Here everyone the relaxed rung would let back in also fails 8+ years, so the next rung is where the count changes. Logging which rung added hits helps tune the order.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
question: A CP-SAT run with max_time_in_seconds = 60 returns FEASIBLE with objective 140. What do you know?
options: 140 is the optimal objective, because the solver stopped
There is a valid solution with objective 140, but a better one may exist
The model is infeasible but a partial solution was returned
The solver crashed and the values are undefined
explain: FEASIBLE means a solution satisfying every constraint was found, but the search ended (here by the time limit) before proving no better one exists. Check the reported best bound to see how far from optimal you might be, or raise the limit.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: cgroup v2: cpu.max throttling and memory.max kills
question: Which pairing correctly matches a cgroup v2 limit to what happens when a workload pushes past it?
options: cpu.max kills the process; memory.max throttles it
cpu.max stalls the threads until the next period; memory.max reclaims first, then OOM kills inside the cgroup
Both throttle: allocations are slowed to the configured rate
Both kill: the OOM killer handles CPU overuse as well
explain: CPU is compressible, so the kernel can withhold it and let the workload continue more slowly. Memory is not: once reclaim fails there is nothing left to withhold, so the cgroup's OOM killer runs and memory.events records the oom_kill. memory.high is the one memory knob that throttles rather than killing.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
question: Which product is the best fit for explicit slot-based state tracking rather than pure query rewriting?
options: A job search with filters for role, level, location, remote and salary
An open-domain assistant answering follow-up questions about history
A chatbot that summarizes a single uploaded PDF
A spell checker
explain: Slot-based tracking needs a schema of constraints. The job search has one, which puts it on the task-oriented side of the line the CIS survey draws. Open-domain QA has no fixed schema and usually relies on rewriting.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Storing state server-side and measuring it
question: Your app stores only the chat transcript and re-derives state each turn. A user removes the remote filter by clicking its chip, then types *show staff roles too*. What is the likely bug?
options: The click is lost: the re-derived state brings remote back because the transcript still says only remote ones
The query builder crashes on a missing slot
Joint goal accuracy cannot be computed
There is no bug; re-derivation handles UI edits automatically
explain: UI edits are not in the transcript unless you write them there. Re-deriving from text alone resurrects the removed filter. Either log UI events into the history or keep server-side state that the click updates directly.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
question: A lab wants CoTs shown to users to be free of offensive content. Which approach best preserves monitorability?
options: Add a reward penalty whenever the raw CoT contains offensive content
Fine-tune the CoT on curated, polite reasoning traces
Leave the raw CoT unpressured and show users a summary written by a separate model
Shorten the CoT with a length penalty so there is less to filter
explain: Penalizing or curating the raw CoT puts direct pressure on it, which Baker et al. show can teach the model to hide content rather than not have it. A length penalty pushes reasoning into activations. A separate summarizer meets the presentation need while the raw CoT stays free for monitoring.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
question: A GPU reports asyncEngineCount = 1. You run two streams, each doing an H2D copy and a kernel. What overlap can you expect?
options: The two H2D copies run concurrently with each other and with the kernels
No overlap at all; one copy engine means strictly serial execution
Copies overlap only if both source buffers are in the same pinned allocation
One H2D copy at a time, but a copy can overlap with a kernel
explain: The best practices guide ties this to asyncEngineCount: a GPU with one copy engine can perform one transfer and execute kernels concurrently, while two copy engines additionally allow a host to device and a device to host transfer at the same time. Streams give permission to overlap; the engine count caps how much overlap the hardware can deliver.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
question: A team wants to replace their bi-encoder with a cross-encoder for first-stage retrieval over 20 million passages. What is the core problem?
options: Cross-encoders cannot handle passages longer than a sentence
Every query would need 20 million transformer forward passes, because no document computation can be done ahead of time
Cross-encoders need the documents to be pre-embedded with the same model first
Cross-encoders only work with BM25 candidates
explain: The cross-encoder's document token states depend on the query, so nothing can be precomputed. Scoring a full corpus means one forward pass per document per query, which is why it is used only on a shortlist from a first stage.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
question: In the listwise softmax view, which candidate in our group receives the largest gradient pushing its score down?
options: The easy negative at -4.0
The positive at 2.0
The hard negative at 1.5
All negatives receive equal gradient
explain: For softmax cross-entropy the gradient on each negative's logit is its probability: 0.331 for z = 1.5, 0.122 for 0.5 and 0.001 for the easy one. The loss focuses on whichever negatives currently compete with the positive.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
question: In the CuTe GEMM tutorial, a CTA calls local_tile(mA, tiler, coord) and each thread then calls local_partition(gA, tA, threadIdx.x). What does each call keep?
options: local_tile keeps the tile mode and slices the rest; local_partition slices the tile mode and keeps the rest
Both keep the tile mode
local_tile keeps the rest mode; local_partition keeps the tile mode
Both keep the rest mode
explain: local_tile (inner partition) indexes the rest mode with the CTA coordinate and keeps one whole tile. local_partition (outer partition) indexes inside the tile with the thread index and keeps the repeats, so a thread gets one element per repeat of the thread tile.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
question: A host has all 64 cores rented to VMs and 100 GB of DRAM still free. Which statement is correct?
options: The 100 GB is stranded: no core is left to pair with it, so it cannot be rented until a VM leaves
The 100 GB is fine: the next VM to arrive can use it
The 100 GB will be swapped out to free space for other hosts
The 100 GB is lost only if the host is a NUMA machine
explain: VMs need cores and memory together. With zero free cores, no new VM fits on this host, so the free DRAM is paid for but unsellable. That is the definition of stranded memory that motivates pooling.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: With demotion enabled, a server's local DRAM node hits its low watermark. What happens to a cold anonymous page that would previously have gone to swap?
options: It is migrated to the CXL node and stays mapped, so a later access is a slower load rather than a page-in from disk
It is compressed into zswap on the local node
It is dropped and re-read from the executable file
It is moved to the CXL node but unmapped until a page fault brings it back to DRAM
explain: Demotion uses page migration in the reclaim path: the page moves to the next slower tier and the page tables are updated. The program can still load it directly, just with CXL latency.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
question: Which step of DoReMi needs the Group DRO optimizer?
options: Only step 3, the large main model
Steps 1 and 3
All three steps
Only step 2, the small proxy model
explain: Step 1 is ordinary training of the reference model, and step 3 is ordinary training of the main model on resampled data. Only the small proxy in step 2 uses the min-max objective, which is why the expensive run needs no special code.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
question: Which workload is the best fit for keeping AoS?
options: Summing one numeric field over every row
Finding all records whose flag byte is set
Fetching a random record by id and returning all of its fields
Running the same arithmetic on x, y and z of every point with SIMD
explain: Random access to whole records uses every byte of the one line AoS brings in, while SoA would touch one line per field. The other three stream a few fields over many records, which is exactly where SoA (or blocked SoA for SIMD) wins.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
question: A kernel sums 4096 float32 products. You pin the reduction so that every run uses the same tree in the same order. What have you guaranteed?
options: The result now equals the exact mathematical sum.
The same inputs give the same bits on every run of the same build and hardware, although the result is still not the exact sum.
The result is now within one ulp of the exact sum.
Any other implementation of the same sum will now agree with you bitwise.
explain: Fixing the order buys reproducibility, not accuracy. The rounding errors are still there; they are simply the same errors every time. A different kernel with a different tree is equally valid IEEE 754 and will generally give different bits.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
question: A cached and an uncached run emit different token ids but detokenize to the same text. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The cache is broken and the test should fail.
The test should only ever compare at the text level, since text is what users receive.
Users are unaffected, but the numerics genuinely differ, so a logit-level or bitwise test is the one that will localize the cause.
The tokenizer is nondeterministic and should be reseeded.
explain: Identical text with different ids is possible, so text equality is the weakest of the three levels. It is the right contract to promise a user and the wrong instrument for finding the cause, which lives in the logits. Compare at the logit level to localize, then state the guarantee at the level you actually promise.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Knowing a run went wrong: invariants, oracles and liveness
question: Your DST suite injects only crashes that always restart within 2 simulated seconds and partitions that always heal within 5. Which bug is it most likely to miss?
options: Two leaders committing different values in the same term
A follower that never catches up while one peer stays permanently down
A torn write corrupting the log
An off-by-one in log index comparison
explain: That is a liveness bug, and it hides whenever faults heal on their own, exactly as in TigerBeetle's resonance bug. The other options are safety violations that can show up under transient faults. To catch liveness bugs, make some faults permanent and require a healthy quorum to keep making progress.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
question: Spot the bug: a colleague's loss is `(ce * masked).sum() / masked.sum()`, the plain average over masked tokens, with t still drawn uniformly. What changes?
options: Nothing; it is the same quantity
The loss now includes visible tokens

Summed over the batch and divided by the total masked count, every masked token gets equal weight, so heavily masked sequences dominate; the 1/t factor is lost and it is no longer the likelihood bound
The model will learn to predict [MASK] tokens
explain: Over a large batch the ratio tends to E[sum of masked losses] / E[count]: the unweighted MaskGIT-style objective with no 1/t, which LLaDA notes lacks a link to maximum likelihood. The principled loss divides each sequence by t L. Dividing each sequence by its own masked count would actually be fine: with uniform t the count is uniform on 0 to L, giving the exact-count form LLaDA uses for likelihoods.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
question: System A serves 9 req/s on 3 GPUs at 92% attainment. System B serves 4 req/s on 1 GPU at 91% attainment, and 4.5 req/s at 85%. Assuming these are the largest rates meeting 90%, which has higher per-GPU goodput?
options: A, because 9 req/s is more than 4 req/s
B, with 4.5 req/s per GPU
They tie, since both exceed 90%
B, with 4 req/s per GPU against A's 3
explain: Per-GPU goodput divides the highest rate meeting the attainment goal by the GPU count: A gives 9/3 = 3 req/s per GPU and B gives 4/1 = 4. B's 4.5 req/s point misses the 90% goal, so it does not count.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes
question: Why does DiskANN keep PQ codes for every point in RAM instead of reading vectors from the SSD to compute distances during the search?
options: Each neighbor's distance would then cost its own random read, multiplying I/O by the degree
PQ distances are exact
The SSD cannot store full vectors
RAM is cheaper than SSD
explain: Search must score every neighbor of every expanded node, which is dozens of distance computations per hop. Fetching each neighbor's vector from SSD would be a random read per neighbor. Approximate PQ distances in RAM steer the search; exact vectors are only needed for the nodes actually read.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA: a fixed-degree graph built for GPUs
question: A CAGRA graph built with intermediate degree 128 and graph degree 64 gives too low recall even with large search settings. Per the cuVS tuning guide, what is the build-side knob to try after graph_degree?
options: Lower intermediate_graph_degree
Disable reverse edges
Increase intermediate_graph_degree, giving pruning more choices
Set alpha = 1.2
explain: cuVS suggests tuning itopk_size first, then graph_degree, then intermediate_graph_degree if graph quality is still too low. A larger kNN graph gives the pruning step more candidates, at a higher build cost. CAGRA has no alpha parameter.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
question: Why does DPO's regularization fail on a pair that appears once in the data?
options: Because DPO forgets to load the reference model
Because the empirical preference for that pair is 1, and fitting probability 1 with a sigmoid needs an unbounded log-ratio gap regardless of beta
Because beta is too large by default
Because the gradient weight grows as the margin grows
explain: One label means the observed preference is 1. The logistic loss can always be lowered further by widening the gap, so the optimum sits at infinity and beta only changes the speed. The weight actually shrinks with the margin; that slows drift but never stops it.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: How dual writes silently diverge, and how to contain it
question: A dual write does `old.increment(counter, 1)` then `new.increment(counter, 1)`, retrying the second call on timeout. After a week the new counters are slightly *higher* than the old ones. What is the most likely cause?
options: Clock skew between the two stores
A timed-out increment had actually been applied, so the retry applied it twice
The backfill copied counters that were already migrated
Last-writer-wins dropped some increments in the old store
explain: A timeout does not mean the write failed. Retrying a non-idempotent delta (add 1) after an ambiguous failure double-applies it. Writing the full current value read from the source of truth, or making the operation idempotent with a request ID, removes the problem.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
question: Why is a kernel module a poor way to add ad hoc tracing to a production machine, compared with an eBPF program?
options: A module cannot read kernel function arguments
Nothing checks the module's code before it runs, so one bad pointer or endless loop can crash or hang the whole machine
Modules can only be loaded at boot time
Modules run in user space and are therefore slow
explain: Modules run arbitrary native code in the kernel with no load-time safety proof. eBPF programs are verified first (termination, initialized registers, in-bounds memory) and only then JIT-compiled and attached.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel
question: Many CPUs increment the same counter. Why does bpftrace recommend @c = count() over @c++?
options: count() uses per-CPU slots, so concurrent updates never collide; @c++ is a non-atomic shared update that can lose increments
@c++ is rejected by the verifier
count() is faster to read than @c++
@c++ sends an event to user space each time
explain: Per-CPU maps make writes cheap and exact. The trade is that reading the value is slower, since every CPU's slot must be summed.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Integer-only inference: int8 multiplies, int32 accumulators
question: A team accumulates int8 x int8 products in an int16 register to save space. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, products of 8-bit numbers always fit in 16 bits
Sums overflow: one product can reach about 32,000, so two products can already exceed the int16 maximum
The zero point can no longer be represented
The scale M stops being in (0, 1)
explain: A single product fits in 16 bits, but the dot product adds hundreds or thousands of them. Jacob et al. use an int32 accumulator for exactly this reason. ONNX Runtime documents a related saturation issue for the VPMADDUBSW instruction on AVX2 and AVX-512, where an intermediate result must fit in 16 bits and is otherwise clamped.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
question: Why do Chen et al. measure outcome efficiency instead of just counting tokens?
options: Token counts cannot be compared across tokenizers
Outcome efficiency rewards models for being short even when they are wrong
It separates tokens that led to the first correct answer from tokens spent after it, so a long but necessary trace is not penalized
It is the metric the models were trained on
explain: A 3,000-token AIME solution that is correct only at the end has efficiency near 1. A 900-token answer to 2 + 3 that was right after 39 tokens scores 4.3%. Raw length cannot tell these apart.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
question: At minute 47 the meter reads 122 W. Which statement is correct using only that one reading?
options: It must be the fridge, because the fridge draws 120 W
It could be the fridge alone, or two 60 W lamps if the house had two, so one reading cannot decide
It must be the lamp plus 62 W of noise
It is the kettle in a low-power state
explain: A single reading only constrains the sum. With three known appliances, 120 W happens to match one combination, but adding a second 60 W lamp would create a second exact match. Context over time (what changed, and when) is what breaks such ties.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
question: A model reaches F1 0.95 on houses it was trained on and 0.60 on a new house. What is the most useful next step suggested by this course's sources?
options: Report 0.95, since the training houses are representative
Shrink the window to one sample to avoid overfitting
Switch to CO, which needs no training data
Add synthetic aggregates built from activations of many houses and evaluate on a held-out house
explain: Kelly and Knottenbelt found that mixing synthetic aggregates with real data regularised the nets and helped on unseen houses, and both they and Zhang and colleagues test on a held-out house. A one-sample window throws away the context that makes neural NILM work, and CO still needs appliance models learned from sub-metered data.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
question: Why is a missing domain scored as weight 0 rather than with the disagree weight -2.74?
options: Missing data carries no evidence either way; scoring it as disagreement would push true duplicates like r1-r3 toward non-match
Because log2 of zero is undefined
Because Fellegi-Sunter only allows agreement levels
explain: A missing value is neither agreement nor disagreement. Treating it as disagreement subtracts 2.74 and would drop r1-r3 from 0.863 to about 0.49, punishing incomplete records rather than conflicting ones.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Inside epoll: interest list, ready list, epoll_wait
question: A loop calls epoll_wait(ep, evs, 64, -1). 200 sockets are ready. What happens to the 136 that do not fit?
options: They are dropped and will not be reported again until new data arrives
They stay ready; later epoll_wait calls round-robin through them
epoll_wait fails with EINVAL because maxevents is too small
The kernel grows the evs array to 200 entries
explain: maxevents only limits how many entries one call copies out. The epoll_wait(2) notes say successive calls round-robin through the ready set, precisely so a few busy descriptors cannot starve the rest.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
question: In the toy, what happens to the expected inflation of the best-of-100 winner if you keep N = 100 but grow the public set from 50 to 200 queries?
options: It roughly halves, because the noise in each system's mean scales like 1/sqrt(n)
It drops to about a quarter, because inflation scales like 1/n
It stays the same, because the number of systems is unchanged
It grows, because more queries give more chances to get lucky
explain: Each system's mean has noise of about s/sqrt(n). Four times as many queries halves that standard deviation, and the expected maximum of 100 draws halves with it. Selection bias shrinks with more queries but never vanishes while you keep selecting.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
question: With 64-byte lines, which pair of 8-byte variables can falsely share a line?
options: A at 0x2000 and B at 0x2040
A at 0x2038 and B at 0x2040
A at 0x2010 and B at 0x2030
A at 0x2000 and B at 0x2080
explain: Divide by 64: 0x2010 and 0x2030 are both in line 0x80 (offsets 16 and 48). 0x2038 is in line 0x80 but 0x2040 starts line 0x81, so adjacent addresses can still be on different lines. Distance alone does not decide it; the line boundary does.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
question: A queue pads head and tail to 64 bytes each, yet still scales badly on x86-64. `perf c2c report --double-cl` shows heavy HITMs on one line pair: offset 0x0 written by `push` threads and 0x40 by `pop` threads. Likely cause?
options: True sharing on one variable
A compiler bug
False sharing caused by adjacent-line prefetching, since 0x0 and 0x40 are neighboring 64-byte lines
The two functions are on the same core
explain: Offsets 0x0 and 0x40 are 64 bytes apart, so with 64-byte lines they are different lines. When they still show up together, the adjacent-line (spatial) prefetcher pairing is the suspect; perf c2c's --double-cl option groups lines in pairs for exactly this. Padding to 128, as crossbeam and folly do on x86-64, is the usual fix.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
question: On the skewed split with E = 5, FedAvg flattens out at 1.944 while the optimum is 2.3. What is the single most reliable fix if you must keep that exact data split?
options: Raise the client fraction C so more clients report each round
Train for ten times as many rounds at E = 5
Do less local work per round (smaller E) or correct the local gradients, which both reduce drift
Increase the local learning rate so clients get closer to their local optima
explain: 1.944 is a fixed point, so more rounds change nothing, and all three clients already report every round so C is irrelevant here. Getting closer to the local optima makes the drift worse: that is the E tending to infinity limit of 1.667. Reducing local work or correcting the local direction (FedProx, SCAFFOLD) attacks the actual cause.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma
question: Why does ACORN-gamma skip HNSW's RNG-based pruning when building neighbor lists?
options: It makes construction too slow
The pruned detour through a third node may fail the predicate, so the shortcut it relied on vanishes in the predicate subgraph
RNG pruning only works for cosine distance
HNSW never prunes at the bottom level
explain: HNSW drops edge v to b if some kept neighbor a is closer to b, trusting search to go v, a, b. For a predicate where v and b pass but a fails, that path does not exist. Without knowing predicates at build time you cannot prune safely, so ACORN keeps the near neighbors and uses a predicate-agnostic compression instead.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Shared experts: an always-on path for common knowledge
question: A team configures 2 shared + 64 routed quarter-size experts and routes to 8 routed experts, keeping the same 2 shared. Compared with DeepSeekMoE 16B (2 + 6 active), what changed?
options: Nothing; shared experts do not count toward compute
Total parameters rose by 2 experts
Activated expert compute rose from 8 to 10 quarter-experts, i.e. from 2 to 2.5 standard FFNs per token
Only the router cost changed
explain: Shared experts always run, so they count fully toward activated compute. DeepSeekMoE lowers the routed top-K by $K_s$ to keep compute fixed: 2 + 6 = 8 quarter-size experts = 2 FFNs. Using 2 + 8 means 10 quarters = 2.5 FFNs, 25% more expert FLOPs.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3: producer and consumer warps, then ping-pong
question: In ping-pong scheduling, what is warpgroup 2 doing while warpgroup 1 computes its softmax?
options: Waiting at a barrier until warpgroup 1 finishes
Running its GEMMs (PV of one iteration and QK of the next) on the tensor cores
Issuing TMA loads for the next K and V tiles
Computing its own softmax on the multi-function unit
explain: The barriers order the two warpgroups' GEMMs so that one warpgroup's slow softmax (exp on MUFU) lands under the other's tensor-core work. Loading is the producer warpgroup's job, and running both softmaxes at once would just make them compete for MUFU.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
question: A decode step for Llama-style GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads. Ignoring other effects, how much does GQA raise attention's operational intensity over plain multi-head attention with the same query count?
options: About 4x, because each KV head serves $g = 4$ query heads
Not at all, decode is always $O(1)$
About 32x, one per query head
It depends only on the page size
explain: The group size is $g = H_{qo}/H_{kv} = 32/8 = 4$. Each key and value loaded from HBM is reused by 4 query heads, so intensity becomes $O(g \cdot l_{qo}) = O(4)$. Page size changes how KV is addressed, not how often each byte is reused.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
question: A batch has average query length 3 per request and GQA group size 8. Which query tile size does FlashInfer's heuristic choose?
options: 32, the smallest tile of at least 3 x 8 = 24 rows
1, because it is mostly decode
16, the smallest Tensor Core tile
128, the prefill default
explain: With head-group fusion the effective query length is $3 \cdot 8 = 24$ rows. The rule takes the smallest tile meeting or exceeding it among 1, 16, 32, 64, 128, which is 32. Choosing 16 would need two tiles; 128 would waste most of the rows.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Reflow and OT couplings: making the paths straight
question: A team has a large text-to-image flow model and a tight compute budget. Which is the main cost they accept if they choose reflow over minibatch OT-CFM?
options: Reflow changes the data distribution the model generates
Reflow requires simulating the first model to generate many training pairs and then a second training run
Reflow cannot be combined with Euler sampling
Reflow increases transport cost
explain: Reflow preserves marginals and does not increase convex transport costs, but each round needs a trained model, a large batch of ODE simulations to create pairs, and another training run. Minibatch OT only re-pairs samples inside each training batch.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLC: breadth-first search over every reachable state
question: TLC reports "Model checking completed. No error has been found" for the counter fixed with an atomic increment, with N = 3. What have you established?
options: Every behavior of the 3-process model satisfies Correct; larger N is unchecked
The fixed algorithm is correct for every number of processes
The Rust implementation of the counter is race-free
The algorithm terminates under every scheduler
explain: TLC is exhaustive only for the finite model you gave it, and only for the properties you listed. It says nothing about code, and termination was not checked (and without fairness it would fail). Proving all N needs a proof, for example with TLAPS.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
question: With delayed scaling, the scale for step t comes from amaxes recorded up to step t-1. A layer's activations suddenly grow 4x at step t. What happens at step t?
options: Training stops with a NaN because E4M3 has no infinity
The largest values exceed 448 after scaling and saturate to 448, so they are clipped for that step
TE detects the overflow and skips the optimizer step
Nothing: the scale is recomputed from step t before casting
explain: Delayed scaling reacts one step late. At step t the old scale pushes the large values past 448 and they saturate (clip). The new amax enters the history, so step t+1 uses a smaller scale. Current scaling avoids this lag at the cost of an extra pass over the tensor.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Pretraining in NVFP4: the four-part recipe and its results
question: A team trains a model with every linear layer in NVFP4 and the run diverges. Following the NVFP4 report, what should they try first?
options: Lower the learning rate by 10x
Move the final few blocks' linear layers (around 15% of the network) back to BF16 or MXFP8
Switch the block size from 16 to 32
Disable the per-tensor FP32 scale
explain: The report found that quantizing all linear layers to FP4 diverged, with the final layers the most sensitive. Keeping the last blocks in higher precision fixed it; even keeping only the final four blocks was stable in their ablation.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: When fsync lies or fails: drive caches and fsyncgate
question: A checkpointer's fsync of a data file returns EIO. Which response is safe on Linux?
options: Call fsync again until it returns 0, then continue
Crash deliberately and replay the WAL from the last checkpoint
Close the file, reopen it and fsync the new descriptor
Ignore it: the next checkpoint will write the page again
explain: The failed pages may already be marked clean and dropped, so a retry can report success with the data lost, and a fresh descriptor may not see the old error at all. The WAL still holds every change since the last checkpoint, so redo can rebuild the pages.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Jaro-Winkler, trigrams and token scorers on the same pairs
question: Using the Jaro-Winkler formula with p = 0.1: `dwayne` vs `duane` has Jaro similarity 0.8222 and shares only the first letter. What is the Jaro-Winkler score?
options: 0.8222, because a prefix of 1 earns no boost
explain: JW = J + l x p x (1 - J) = 0.8222 + 1 x 0.1 x 0.1778 = 0.8400. Every shared leading character (up to 4) moves the score a tenth of the remaining distance toward 1.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
question: Why does the table store each model under *all* ordered basis pairs rather than just one canonical pair?
options: To make the table smaller
Because the canonical pair might be hidden or missing in the scene, and any visible pair must still be able to find the model
Because a single pair does not define a frame under similarity transforms
To avoid quantization errors at bin edges
explain: Occlusion and clutter are the whole point. If only basis (p1, p2) were stored and p1 were hidden, the model could never be found. Storing all n(n-1) bases means any two visible model points can serve as the scene basis.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
question: You have hundreds of frames of the same field from one night and want to stack them. Which approach fits best?
options: Blind-solve each frame against an all-sky quad index, every time
Use SIFT descriptors on the star patches
Register frames to each other with triangle asterism matching (as in astroalign), solving just one frame blind if you need sky coordinates
Assume the frames are already aligned
explain: Frame-to-frame registration has a tiny search space, where triangle matching plus RANSAC is fast and reliable. Blind all-sky solving is for when you do not know where the image points; doing it per frame is wasteful.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
question: A teammate's 'nearby drivers' query returns all drivers whose geohash starts with the rider's 6-character geohash, then sorts by haversine distance. Riders near cell edges complain that close drivers never appear. What is the bug?
options: Haversine is inaccurate under 1 km and should be replaced by Euclidean distance
Geohash should be computed latitude first, not longitude first
Only the center cell is searched, so drivers in the 8 neighboring cells are never candidates
The prefix should be longer so cells are smaller
explain: Candidate generation must cover the whole circle. A rider near an edge has close drivers in neighboring cells, which share a shorter prefix or none at all. A longer prefix makes it worse; the fix is the center cell plus its 8 neighbors at a precision matched to the radius.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row
question: Dropping the minus one half from the source coordinate produces a shift of (s - 1) / 2 source pixels. When is that shift exactly zero?
options: When the output is larger than the source
Only when s = 1, that is when the output size equals the source size
When s is an integer, because the taps land on pixel centers
When nearest neighbour is used instead of bilinear
explain: The expression (s - 1) / 2 vanishes only at s = 1. Integer scale factors are the worst case for visibility, not the safe case: at s = 2 the shift is half a source pixel and at s = 4 it is 1.5 source pixels. Upscaling gives a negative shift, not zero.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Batching: why 32 launches lose to one
question: In a var-shape batch, the grid's x and y dimensions are sized from the largest image. What follows?
options: Blocks are launched for every image as if it were the largest, so a single outlier makes most blocks exit immediately at the bounds check
Smaller images are padded to the largest size before the kernel runs
The kernel must be launched once per distinct image size
Each image gets its own grid, so there is no waste
explain: z indexes the image and x and y tile the largest output, so every image's slice of the grid is as wide as the biggest one. For one 1920x1080 image among 31 small crops that is 65280 blocks launched against 3559 useful ones. No padding happens and the launch stays single: the waste is empty blocks, which is why batches are usually bucketed by size.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Expandable segments: growing one segment with virtual memory
question: In the fixed-segment toy, why could release_cached_blocks not rescue the Y2 allocation?
options: Because release_cached_blocks only works on the small pool
Because the device was out of virtual address space
Because Y2 was on a different stream
Because all cached free memory was inside segments that also held live tensors, and only whole unsplit segments can be released
explain: cudaFree releases a whole segment. Segments 1 to 3 each held a live 22 MiB tensor next to a 2 MiB hole, so none could be returned. The 22 MiB of unreserved memory alone was too small.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Misalignment, strides and effective bandwidth
question: Why did the V100 offsetCopy measurement lose only about 10% instead of the 20% the sector count predicts?
options: The V100 hardware realigns misaligned addresses for free
cudaMalloc pads arrays so that offsets never cross a sector
Adjacent warps reuse the over-fetched boundary sectors from cache
The kernel was limited by arithmetic, not memory
explain: Each warp's fifth sector is the next warp's first. The Best Practices Guide attributes the 9/10 result to adjacent warps reusing cache lines their neighbors fetched.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
question: On an H100, a kernel uses 256-thread blocks, 40 registers per thread and 32 KB of shared memory per block. Which resource limits occupancy?
options: Shared memory: 228/32 allows 7 blocks
Registers: 10,240 registers per block allows 6 blocks, fewer than the 7 that shared memory and the 8 that thread slots allow
Block slots: 32 resident blocks per SM
Nothing: the configuration reaches 100 percent occupancy
explain: Thread slots allow 2048/256 = 8 blocks; shared memory allows 228/32 = 7; registers need 40 x 32 = 1280 per warp and 8 x 1280 = 10,240 per block, so 65,536/10,240 = 6. The minimum is 6 blocks, 48 warps, 75 percent, and the limiter is the register file. Nsight Compute would show the same split across launch__occupancy_limit_registers, _shared_mem and _warps.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Computing a thread's global index: vector add end to end
question: A kernel uses `int i = threadIdx.x + blockDim.x * blockIdx.x;` and is launched with 4,000 blocks of 256 threads on an array of 1,000,000 floats, with no bounds check. What happens?
options: Fine: 4,000 x 256 is close enough to one million
Threads with i from 1,000,000 to 1,023,999 access memory past the end of the arrays
Only the first 3,907 blocks run; the runtime drops the rest automatically
The compiler inserts the bounds check because N is known
explain: 4,000 x 256 = 1,024,000 threads, so 24,000 threads have an index at or beyond N. Only 3907 blocks were needed (ceil of 1,000,000 / 256), and even then the last block would have 192 idle threads that need the `if (i < N)` check. Nothing drops blocks or adds checks for you.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: The same model in Metal: threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch
question: A Metal kernel assumes a SIMD-group is 32 wide and uses `thread_index_in_threadgroup / 32` to pick a SIMD-group's slot in threadgroup memory. What is the portable fix?
options: Nothing: every Metal GPU uses 32-wide SIMD-groups by specification
Use [[thread_position_in_grid]] / 32
Add threadgroup_barrier before the division
Use [[simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup]] (or divide by threads_per_simdgroup) instead of the constant 32
explain: MSL defines the SIMD-group width as a property you query (threads_per_simdgroup, or threadExecutionWidth on the host) and says the threadgroup is divided into SIMD-groups in an implementation-defined way. The built-in simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup gives the right answer on any GPU.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
question: You need to answer 200 broad questions a day over the same corpus and cost matters most. Based on the paper's Podcast results, which level is the best starting point?
options: C3, because it is most detailed
TS, because it reads the source text
C0, because it uses about 2.6% of TS's tokens while still beating vector RAG on comprehensiveness and diversity
Vector RAG, because it is cheapest
explain: The paper recommends root-level summaries for repeated global queries: dramatically fewer tokens with a modest drop versus other global methods. Vector RAG is cheapest but loses on comprehensiveness and diversity for these questions.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Why PPO is costly for LLMs and what GRPO removes
question: A colleague says: "GRPO is cheaper because it does not need a reward model." What is the best correction?
options: Correct: GRPO never uses a reward model
GRPO removes the value model (critic); the reward can still come from a learned reward model or from a verifier
GRPO removes the reference model; the critic is still required
GRPO removes the policy's optimizer state by freezing most layers
explain: The saving comes from dropping the critic, a second trained network. DeepSeekMath's GRPO used a learned reward model. Whether the reward is a model or code is the separate RLVR question.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Failure modes and fixes: dead groups, entropy collapse, length bias
question: Halfway through training, 60% of your prompts are solved by all 16 samples. What is the most direct fix?
options: Raise the KL coefficient
Filter out groups whose rewards are all equal and keep sampling until the batch has enough informative groups (dynamic sampling), or add harder prompts
Lower the learning rate
Divide advantages by the response length
explain: All-correct groups have zero advantage and contribute no gradient, so 60% of your rollouts are wasted. Dynamic sampling refills the batch with mixed-outcome groups; a harder curriculum attacks the cause.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
question: A consumer joins TripUpdates to the schedule using only trip_id. For a daily train with trip_id N8 departing 20:00, the producer sends an update for yesterday's N8, now running 14 hours late. What breaks?
options: Nothing, delays over 12 hours are discarded by protobuf
The feed is rejected because delay must be under 3600 s
The update cannot be applied because it has no stop_id
The update is applied to today's N8, so riders see a wrong prediction
